problem: Existing path planners (A*, etc.) and socially aware navigation methods optimize distance or human comfort and lack semantic understanding of the whole environment, so they ignore privacy exposure when a robot carries sensitive objects through crowded public spaces.
motivation: Robots transporting sensitive items (e.g. classified files) should avoid heavily populated areas, not just take the shortest path. VLMs carry world knowledge about which rooms are busy, so they can reason over a top-view map and an instruction to pick a more discreet route.
key_idea: Enumerate candidate hallway-based paths from a topological map with DFS and A*, overlay each on a top-view map, and let a VLM (GPT-4 Turbo) pick the most privacy-preserving one via zero-shot CoT and majority voting.
insight: Privacy-aware selection trades path length for lower exposure: the VLM picks longer routes that bypass office areas, cutting P_risk by roughly 35-53% versus A* in the reported table. Only a baseline comparison is given, with no ablations of the VLM, prompts or voting, so the sources of the gain are not isolated. The evaluation metric is a Gaussian-modulated distance field, which is not independent of the map-based reasoning the VLM does.
method: Metric maps: build a top-view map (highest point per cell, ceilings removed) and a traversability map from the point cloud
Topological map: nodes are annotated rooms, with edges only between hallway nodes and other rooms by minimum point-cloud distance

Path generation: DFS extracts all simple paths, filters to hallway-only paths and removes subpath supersets, keeps the top-k shortest, then runs A* between neighboring node centers on the traversability map
Optimal path inference: each candidate path is drawn on the top-view map with an ID and fed with the instruction to GPT-4 Turbo using zero-shot CoT, and five independent runs are majority-voted
Evaluation metric: P_risk is the sum of Gaussian-modulated FMM distance-field values along the path, computed with office/conference rooms as obstacles
Real-world deployment: a scanned iPad point cloud is aligned to a Gmapping map on a Jackal robot, and the ROS navigation stack follows the topological path

setting.observation: pre-built 3D point cloud map (top-view and traversability maps) plus text instruction; real robot uses lidar for localization
setting.action_space: global path selection among candidate A* metric paths, followed by ROS navigation stack
setting.simulator: none (offline evaluation on S3DIS point clouds); real world with ROS
setting.privileged: known full environment map with semantic room annotations; manually marked topological nodes in the real scene

numbers_note: Custom benchmark with 9 episodes total. The text reports Area_5a P_risk as 1,804.972 while the table says 1564.794. No standard navigation benchmark was used.
results: On three S3DIS areas, PANav lowers P_risk versus A* (Area_3 960.534 vs 1928.649; Area_4 321.152 vs 682.212; Area_5a 1564.794 vs 2390.677) at the cost of longer paths (e.g. 4973 vs 3373). A real-world Jackal robot demo in an office chose the longer, less crowded path.
limitations: Tiny evaluation (9 episodes, 3 areas), only an A* baseline, no ablations, and text/table inconsistency for Area_5a
Assumes a known static map with manual topological nodes and alignment; no dynamic humans
Privacy risk metric is a distance-field proxy rather than real human presence or a human study
